power.title: Power Analysis Check
report: No power analyses were detected.

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. Metacheck does not yet analyze automatically whether sentences which include non-significant p-values are correct, but we recommend manually checking the sentences below for possible misinterpreted non-significant p values. ```{r} #| echo: false # table data -------------------------------------- table <- structure(list(Text = c("p=0.54", "p=1.0"), Sentence = c("Older patients are not scarce (Emory: 205,701 ECGs at ≥75), and increasing the labelled set from 3,000 ECGs to the full set raised AUROC by 0.016 (p=0.0001) but changed the gap by only -0.010 (Holm-adjusted p=0.54; Fig. 4B).", "Group-robust optimisation [23], class balancing, per-age-band probes and focal reweighting changed the gap by medians of +0.000, +0.000, +0.003 and +0.002 (all adjusted p=1.0) while costing overall AUROC (-0.005 to -0.171; Fig. 4C), and a non-linear per-band read-out never recovered the oldest band (avoidable gain -0.025 to -0.001; Fig. 4D)." )), row.names = c(NA, -2L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame" )) # display table ----------------------------------- metacheck::report_table(table, c(0.1, 0.9), 10, FALSE) ``` ::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} For metascientific articles demonstrating the rate of misinterpretations of non-significant results is high, see: Aczel B, Palfi B, Szollosi A, Kovacs M, Szaszi B, Szecsi P, Zrubka M, Gronau Q, van den Bergh D, Wagenmakers E (2018). “Quantifying Support for the Null Hypothesis in Psychology: An Empirical Investigation.” Advances in Methods and Practices in Psychological Science, 1(3), 357–366. doi:10.1177/2515245918773742. Murphy S, Merz R, Reimann L, Fernández A (2025). “Nonsignificance misinterpreted as an effect’s absence in psychology: Prevalence and temporal analyses.” Royal Society Open Science, 12(3), 242167. doi:10.1098/rsos.242167. For educational material on preventing the misinterpretation of p values, see [Improving Your Statistical Inferences](https://lakens.github.io/statistical_inferences/01-pvalue.html#sec-misconception1). :::

codebook_check.title: Codebook Check
codebook_check.summary_text:
-  We parsed 410 variable definitions from codebook/README files.
-  1 of 2856 data columns (0%) is documented in a codebook; 2855 are not.
-  A codebook was found and parsed (410 variable definitions), but its variable names do not match the data columns, so the documentation could not be linked automatically (only 0% of columns matched). For example, the codebook documents ``panel``, ``backbone``, ``backbone_label`` while the data has `arch`, `median_seed_sd`, `max_seed_sd`. This often means the data holds computed scores or subscales while the codebook lists the underlying items. To make the codebook usable automatically, document variables under the exact names used in the data file (one row per data column), with a label and, for rating items, the response scale.

#### Files that do not belong in the repository

We left out 554 files that software creates by itself, not the authors: operating system (554). They hold nothing a reader can use, but they clutter the repository, and software can mistake them for real files (for example a `._` copy of a `.csv` for data).

*Remove these:* *Operating system* files: macOS adds a `__MACOSX` folder and a `._` copy of every file it puts in a zip, and `.DS_Store` files to folders; Windows adds `Thumbs.db` and `desktop.ini`. On a Mac, create zips from the command line with `zip -r -X`, or remove them afterwards with `zip -d archive.zip "__MACOSX/*" "*.DS_Store"`. *RStudio session files* (`.Rproj.user/`) hold open tabs and unsaved edits; *R history* (`.Rhistory`) lists the commands typed in a session and can hold file paths and passwords; *Jupyter checkpoints* (`.ipynb_checkpoints/`) are automatic copies of notebooks; *compiled Python files* (`__pycache__/`, `.pyc`) are recreated when the code runs; *open-document lock files* (`~$...docx`, `.~lock...#`) are left while a document is open; *editor backups* (`file~`, `.bak`, `.swp`) and *temporary files* (`.tmp`, `.temp`) are copies a program made by itself.

*Keep only on purpose:* *version control* folders (`.git`, `.svn`, `.hg`) hold the project's history, which can include earlier versions of files and data that was later removed; *editor settings* (`.idea`, `.vscode`) can hold paths on your own computer. A `.gitignore` based on GitHub's templates (https://github.com/github/gitignore) keeps them out of a repository.

:::

This module runs automated data-quality checks (empty columns, SPSS filter variables, category casing, stray whitespace, numbers stored as text, problematic and colliding column names, mixed text encodings, personal information, spreadsheet formatting, and careless responding) on the extracted data files.
We examined 2856 columns across 174 data files.
#### Issues Identified

76 file/column combinations have at least one issue.

**About the personal-information flags.** These are pattern matches, not confirmed disclosures, and they are tuned to over-report rather than miss something. Expect false positives:

- **Column names** are matched against identifying words in English and other European languages (`email`, `telefoonnummer`, `geboortedatum`, ...). A column called `phone_number` flags whether or not it holds one, and an empty or already-anonymised column flags on its name alone.
- **Values** are matched against the shape of an identifier. An IP address pattern also matches a version string or a dotted numeric code; a card-number pattern requires both a real issuer prefix and a checksum, but a long numeric ID can still coincide.
- **Free text** is flagged when a column holds long, mostly-distinct prose — the shape open-ended answers take. Most such columns contain no names at all.

A flag means *look at this column*. Where the data is already de-identified (an `ip` column reading `Anonymized`, a `name` column the authors emptied), no action is needed.

No file could be screened for careless responding.

**What this does not cover.** Only 0 of 174 data files could be screened: the rest had no detectable multi-item scale block, or too few respondents. Even in a screened file, these checks only look at multi-item rating scales — the only place where a repeated or flat answer pattern is interpretable. Single questions, open text, demographics and any item outside a detected scale block are never examined. A respondent can therefore answer most of a survey carelessly and still not be flagged here, and finding nothing is not evidence that a dataset is free of careless responding.

This module also assesses whether the paper's Python code could be run on its data, and — because `execute = TRUE` — **actually ran it**. We examined 50 Python code files.

#### File paths
**55 data paths in the code do not work in the repository as deposited.** We pointed them to where the file is, so the code could run: `out` to `../fig4_mitigation/disfig/out` (in release_bundle_v1/figS09_lorabands/build.py); `island_figure.py` to `build/island_figure.py` (in release_bundle_v1/figS06_island/build.py); `out` to `../fig4_mitigation/disfig/out` (in release_bundle_v1/figS06_island/build.py); `{R}/island_membership_mimic.csv` to `inputs/island_results/island_membership_mimic.csv` (in island_figure.py); `{R}/island_vs_mainland_stats.csv` to `inputs/island_results/island_vs_mainland_stats.csv` (in island_figure.py); `{R}/umap_common_subsample_coords.csv` to `inputs/island_results/umap_common_subsample_coords.csv` (in island_figure.py); `{R}/island_set_isolation_by_backbone.csv` to `inputs/island_results/island_set_isolation_by_backbone.csv` (in island_figure.py); `{R}/dist_cart_ecgfm.csv` to `inputs/island_results/dist_cart_ecgfm.csv` (in island_figure.py); `out` to `../fig4_mitigation/disfig/out` (in release_bundle_v1/figS20_utility/build.py); `out` to `../fig4_mitigation/disfig/out` (in release_bundle_v1/fig3_embedding/build.py), and 45 more. The code should be changed, because as written it does not find these files. The code reads files that are only inside `supporting_tables.zip`, `figure_source_data_bundles.zip`, and no script unpacks them. We unpacked them in their folder before the run. So that others can run the code as deposited, start the code with a line that unpacks them (such as `zipfile.ZipFile("supporting_tables.zip").extractall()` in Python), or upload the files unpacked.

#### Execution
**The Python code was run.** Each script ran in an isolated Docker container against a throwaway copy of the repository, in the run order above, with a 300-second per-script timeout. Of 50 scripts: 33 ran without error, 15 errored, 0 timed out, 0 could not run because one of its own dependencies is unavailable, 0 did not parse, and 0 are written for Python 2 and not run. 2 files were not run on their own, because other files import them: release_bundle_v1/figS06_island/build/figstyle.py (by island_figure.py); build_classical_figure.py (by release_bundle_v1/figS14_classicalgap/build.py, release_bundle_v1/figS13_classicalbands/build.py). Running against current package versions: a break can reflect version drift, which argues for pinning versions (e.g. in a `requirements.txt`). **6 scripts looked for 7 files in another folder than the deposit has them**, so before running them once more we copied them there: `release_bundle_v1/fig1_cohorts/data/cohort_n_final.json` to `release_bundle_v1/fig1_cohorts/cohort_n_final.json` for `Fig1_study_scope_final.py`; `release_bundle_v1/fig5_controls/r1final/classical/classical_age_band_results.csv` to `release_bundle_v1/inputs/classical_age_band_results.csv` for `release_bundle_v1/figS15_classicalmatched/build.py`; `release_bundle_v1/fig4_mitigation/figure/Fig4.pdf` to `release_bundle_v1/fig4_mitigation/out/Fig4.pdf` for `release_bundle_v1/fig4_mitigation/build.py`; `release_bundle_v1/fig5_controls/figure/Fig5.pdf` to `release_bundle_v1/fig5_controls/out/Fig5.pdf` for `release_bundle_v1/fig5_controls/build.py`; `release_bundle_v1/figS11_null/figure/FigS_null_bands.pdf` to `release_bundle_v1/figS11_null/out/FigS_null_bands.pdf` for `release_bundle_v1/figS11_null/build.py`; `release_bundle_v1/figS04_adjgap/figure/FigS_adjacent_band_gap.pdf` to `release_bundle_v1/figS04_adjgap/out/FigS_adjacent_band_gap.pdf` for `release_bundle_v1/figS04_adjgap/build.py`; `release_bundle_v1/figS15_classicalmatched/figure/FigS_classical_age_matched.png` to `release_bundle_v1/figS15_classicalmatched/out/FigS_classical_age_matched.png` for `release_bundle_v1/figS15_classicalmatched/build.py`. **`os.chdir()` in the code**
**3 scripts call `os.chdir()`.** This is bad practice: it hardcodes where the code must run (often an absolute path on the author's own machine) and breaks the moment the code is run anywhere else. To run the code we replaced these calls with `pass`. Any such script that then ran is **reproducible only after ignoring an `os.chdir()` that should not have been in the code and needs to be fixed**.

text.text: Background.
Electrocardiogram (ECG) foundation models are proposed for clinical use and promoted as fair, yet such claims are rarely tested with subgroup-stratified evaluation.

We measured demographic disparities across four ECG foundation models, tested whether mitigation removes them, and asked whether the dominant disparity originates in the models or in the data and the clinical task.
Methods.

We probed frozen embeddings of four architecturally distinct ECG foundation models (ECGFounder, xECG, ECG-FM, DeepECG-SSL) in thirteen cohorts on four continents (5.4 million analysed ECGs, 31 endpoints, six held-out cohorts), stratified by age, sex and race.

We examined embedding geometry, tested post-hoc correction, larger labelled training sets, comorbidity exclusion and low-rank fine-tuning, and compared each network with an untrained copy of itself and with logistic regression on classical ECG measurements.
Findings.

Disparities concentrated on age, not sex or race (median worst-group AUROC gap 0.028 vs 0.004 and 0.016; age exceeded sex in 97% of results) and replicated externally (ED-BWH 30-day MACE AUROC 0.81-0.90 under 40 years, 0.64-0.71 at ≥75).
Age formed a smooth gradient in the embeddings, whereas sex, though most decodable, carried no gap.
No remedy closed it (low-rank adaptation: -0.007 to -0.004).
Untrained copies (r=0.81, 102 pairs) and classical measurements (ρ=0.90) reproduced the endpoint-specific gaps, and pretraining raised AUROC (+0.067) without changing them.
The largest race effect, higher potassium error in Black patients, vanished at matched true potassium.
Interpretation.
ECG foundation models carry an age-structured disparity that replicates externally and survives mitigation.

Because untrained networks and a classical model reproduce it, the results indicate that it is inherited from the age structure of the ECG and its labels rather than created by the models, so switching or adapting models will not remove it.
Age-stratified reporting, untrained and classical baselines, and age-specific thresholds and recalibration are therefore needed.

Deep learning applied to the 12-lead electrocardiogram has progressed from arrhythmia classification [1] to the inference of conditions with no classical ECG signature, such as left-ventricular dysfunction [2], hyperkalaemia and latent atrial fibrillation [3], and recently to risk markers for sudden cardiac death.
text.formatted: Deep learning applied to the 12-lead electrocardiogram has progressed from arrhythmia classification <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">[1]</ref> to the inference of conditions with no classical ECG signature, such as left-ventricular dysfunction <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">[2]</ref>, hyperkalaemia and latent atrial fibrillation <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">[3]</ref>, and recently to risk markers for sudden cardiac death.

text.text: ECG foundation models [4] [5] [6] [7] now generalise across many such tasks and are increasingly proposed for clinical deployment, with their scale and demographic breadth presented as answering the fairness concerns raised against earlier task-specific models [4], and with fairness analyses restricted to age and sex at a single operating point [7].
text.formatted: ECG foundation models <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">[4]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">[5]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">[6]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">[7]</ref> now generalise across many such tasks and are increasingly proposed for clinical deployment, with their scale and demographic breadth presented as answering the fairness concerns raised against earlier task-specific models <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">[4]</ref>, and with fairness analyses restricted to age and sex at a single operating point <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">[7]</ref>.

text.text: Such claims are rarely supported by discrimination evaluated separately by age, sex and race, so whether these models are equitable where they would be used remains largely uncharacterised.

This matters because fairness failures in clinical machine learning are well documented, from a care-management algorithm that under-served Black patients [8] to under-diagnosis of under-served groups by imaging models [9] and the recovery of self-reported race from images clinicians cannot read [10].
text.formatted: This matters because fairness failures in clinical machine learning are well documented, from a care-management algorithm that under-served Black patients <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">[8]</ref> to under-diagnosis of under-served groups by imaging models <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">[9]</ref> and the recovery of self-reported race from images clinicians cannot read <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">[10]</ref>.

text.text: Foundation models reach clinical tasks most often as frozen feature extractors, where a fixed pretrained backbone produces an embedding that a lightweight probe maps to a clinical label, and increasingly through parameter-efficient fine-tuning of the backbone.

Benchmarks such as OpenECG [11] and BenchECG [6] compare aggregate cross-centre generalisation without stratifying by subgroup, and the one fairness analysis of an ECG foundation model family [7] is confined to two models on their own endpoints, micro-averaged over 77 classes and stratified by age and sex only.
text.formatted: Benchmarks such as OpenECG <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">[11]</ref> and BenchECG <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">[6]</ref> compare aggregate cross-centre generalisation without stratifying by subgroup, and the one fairness analysis of an ECG foundation model family <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">[7]</ref> is confined to two models on their own endpoints, micro-averaged over 77 classes and stratified by age and sex only.

text.text: Prior work has shown that individual, task-trained ECG and cardiac-imaging models carry race, sex and age disparities [9, 12], and that model-side remedies often fail to generalise [13].
text.formatted: Prior work has shown that individual, task-trained ECG and cardiac-imaging models carry race, sex and age disparities <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">[9,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">12]</ref>, and that model-side remedies often fail to generalise <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">[13]</ref>.

text.text: We evaluate four architecturally distinct ECG foundation models (ECGFounder [4], convolutional; xECG [6], recurrent (xLSTM); ECG-FM [5], supervised Transformer; DeepECG-SSL [7], selfsupervised Transformer) under one frozen-probe protocol across thirteen cohorts on four continents, and ask whether low-rank fine-tuning removes any disparity the frozen-probe evaluation reveals.
text.formatted: We evaluate four architecturally distinct ECG foundation models (ECGFounder <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">[4]</ref>, convolutional; xECG <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">[6]</ref>, recurrent (xLSTM); ECG-FM <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">[5]</ref>, supervised Transformer; DeepECG-SSL <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">[7]</ref>, selfsupervised Transformer) under one frozen-probe protocol across thirteen cohorts on four continents, and ask whether low-rank fine-tuning removes any disparity the frozen-probe evaluation reveals.

text.text: Three controls under the identical pipeline go one step further: universal time-series foundation models that have never seen an ECG, an untrained copy of every network, and a logistic regression on classical ECG measurements.
A disparity that appears without ECG pretraining, without any training and without deep learning cannot be a property of the models and must come from the data and the clinical task.

We therefore measure subgroup performance, including on held-out external cohorts, trace the dominant disparity to its substrate in the embedding geometry, test whether mitigation and fine-tuning remove it, and test whether it is present without pretraining or deep learning.
Cohorts and endpoints.

Thirteen de-identified cohorts span four continents (Fig. 1 and Supplementary Table S1): HEEDB-MGH and HEEDB-Emory [14], MIMIC-IV-ECG [15], EchoNext [16] and ED-BWH (United States), CODE [17] and CODE-II (Brazil), PTB-XL [18] (Germany), LEAD [19] (Austria), IKEM (Czechia), and Shaoxing, CPSC2018 and SPHDB (China).

text.text: The analysis sets comprise 5,396,975 ECGs from 2,509,462 patients (curation flows in Supplementary Figs S1-S3).

text.text: The 31 endpoints (Supplementary Table S2) cover rhythm and conduction, structural and ischaemic disease, laboratory values within ±6 h of the ECG, outcomes and chronological age, and each classification endpoint is grouped by how its label is obtained (outcome, coded diagnosis, diagnosis read from the ECG, measurement).

Models and read-out.

We used ECGFounder [4], xECG [6], ECG-FM [5] and DeepECG-SSL [7] with their public weights and native preprocessing (Supplementary Table S4), spanning supervised and self-supervised pretraining, and two universal time-series models never trained on ECGs: TiRex-2 [20], built like xECG on the xLSTM architecture, and MOMENT-1-large [21], a Transformer encoder that processes each lead as a separate series.

text.text: Throughout, pretrained denotes a network with its publicly released weights, which we did not modify except in the low-rank adaptation experiments; untrained denotes the same architecture with random initialisation.
For each backbone, cohort and endpoint we fitted an ℓ 2 -regularised logistic or ridge probe with patient-grouped five-fold out-of-fold prediction, so that every labelled ECG is scored held-out.
We report AUROC (classification) and MAE (regression) overall and by age band (<40, 40-59, 60-74, ≥75 years), sex and race, with 1,000-fold bootstrap 95% CIs.
text.formatted: We report AUROC (classification) and MAE (regression) overall and by age band (<40, 40-59, 60-74, ≥75 years), sex and race, with 1,000-fold bootstrap 95% CIs.

text.text: Race is the category recorded in the source electronic health record (White, Black, Asian; US cohorts only).
The worst-group gap is the best minus the worst subgroup on one axis.
The age gap is AUROC in the youngest minus the oldest band (for MAE, the reverse), so that a positive value means worse performance in older patients.
A secondary definition, AUROC at 40-59 minus ≥75 years, serves endpoints whose youngest band is sparse.
Embedding geometry and attention.

Embeddings were described by UMAP, by a silhouette index of how separated the groups of each attribute are in the embedding space (within-group against nearest-other-group distance; 0 means no structure), and by the decodability of each attribute, the gain in balanced accuracy over chance of a linear probe predicting age band, sex or race from the embedding.
A detached cluster was characterised by HDBSCAN and acquisition metadata.

To ask where the models attend and whether any wave carries the gap, SmoothGrad saliency was computed on delineated beats for the four ECG backbones on eight endpoints, and the P wave, QRS complex or T wave was set to zero and the probe refitted (Supplementary Methods).
Because AF, paced rhythm and bundle-branch block accumulate with age and could carry the gap, age gaps were re-scored after removing ECGs with these findings (never the target condition).
Because a gap could reflect too few labels, probes were trained on 100 to 30 000 labelled ECGs for seven endpoints.

Because it could reflect the capacity or objective of the read-out, on held-out patient-level splits we compared the standard probe with per-age-band readouts, error-focused (focal) reweighting and a per-band gradient-boosted read-out (10 endpoints, four backbones).

Because it could reside in the frozen weights, we compared frozen probes with low-rank adaptation (LoRA [22], rank 8) of each ECG backbone under empirical-risk, group-robust [23] and class-balanced objectives (114 age-stratified cells), each with a paired frozen probe on the identical split.
text.formatted: Because it could reside in the frozen weights, we compared frozen probes with low-rank adaptation (LoRA <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">[22]</ref>, rank 8) of each ECG backbone under empirical-risk, group-robust <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">[23]</ref> and class-balanced objectives (114 age-stratified cells), each with a paired frozen probe on the identical split.

text.text: To test whether the gap requires learned weights at all, each architecture was rebuilt with random initialisation and no loaded weights, and probed exactly as the pretrained model (117 endpoint-backbone pairs, 102 with AUROC endpoints).

MOMENT-1-large, its untrained copy and two further random initialisations of the five networks were run on patient-grouped subsets of at most 100,000 ECGs per cohort, with paired probes on the same ECGs (Supplementary Methods).

To test whether it requires deep learning, logistic regression and gradient-boosted trees were trained under the same folds on 20-48 standard measurements (intervals, durations, axes, amplitudes) and their age gaps compared with the median pretrained gap.

To locate the gap, we computed the AUROC of cases from each age band against controls from each band and, for four endpoints, miss rate, specificity and calibration by age band at a single threshold versus age-specific thresholds chosen on separate patients.

For the potassium race effect we compared errors within 0.25 mmol/L bins of true potassium, standardised the Black error to the White potassium distribution and adjusted for eGFR (Supplementary Methods).
Inference rests on effect sizes with bootstrap 95% CIs (1,000 resamples of ECGs, percentile method) and their consistency across backbones and cohorts.

Hypothesis tests are limited to pre-defined paired comparisons: Wilcoxon signed-rank tests across endpoints for changes under each mitigation strategy, a Mann-Whitney test for the label-type contrast, and Pearson or Spearman correlations for the concordance of gaps between pretrained, untrained and classical models.
All tests are two-sided and Holm-adjusted within each family (Supplementary Table S5).

Across thirteen cohorts on four continents (5.4 million analysed ECGs from 2.51 million patients; Fig. 1), the four backbones reach clinically useful discrimination and agree closely with one another (median range of AUROC across backbones per endpoint 0.015, interquartile range 0.006-0.035; Fig. 2A; Supplementary Tables S8 and S11): frozen-probe AUROC is high on structural endpoints (EchoNext LVEF≤45% 0.824-0.879) and MI (PTB-XL 0.878-0.922), near-ceiling on atrial fibrillation (CODE 0.971-0.981, 2,322,465 ECGs), and moderate on physiological inference (hyperkalaemia 0.653-0.753).

Discrimination declined toward the oldest band on 12 of 16 classification endpoints, was near-identical between the sexes, and varied little by race, with the worst-served race group changing from endpoint to endpoint (White in 31, Asian in 24, Black in 16 of 102 results).
Age gaps of different backbones were closely related across endpoints (pairwise Spearman ρ 0.85-0.95).

If the gap were an artifact of the frozen read-out, of too few labels, or of the comorbid ECGs that accumulate with age, changing those should remove it.

text.text: Letting the backbone move its weights does not reallocate accuracy across age.
The age-dominant, sex-null fingerprint survives every intervention and every architecture, so the disparity is not a tunable property of read-out capacity, label quantity or comorbid case mix.
What can be changed is the operating point.

text.text: Together with the invariance across architectures, objectives and adaptations, these controls indicate that the age gap lies in the age structure of the ECG and of its clinical labels rather than in the models.
Across four ECG foundation models and thirteen cohorts, strong average and external discrimination coexists with a systematic disparity that concentrates on age, not sex or race.
It replicates externally, has a representational substrate and resists every standard remedy.

The same fingerprint is shared by every architecture and pretraining objective, reproduced by two time-series models that have never seen an ECG, by untrained copies of every network and by a logistic regression on classical measurements, and unchanged by larger labelled sets, comorbidity exclusion, alternative read-outs, group-robust objectives or low-rank fine-tuning.
The results therefore indicate that the models inherit this disparity from the age structure of the ECG and of its clinical labels rather than create it.

Three observations say where: the gap is largest for outcome and coded labels, which depend on information the ECG is unlikely to contain; discrimination depends more on the age of the controls than of the cases, because older people without the condition carry ECGs that resemble disease; and the comorbid ECGs we can flag carry only a small part of it.

The second observation is physiology, not artefact: the ECG's age signal is dominated by atrial features that strengthen with hypertension and smoking, and an ECG age ≥8 years above chronological age doubles mortality

text.text: The gap is nonetheless real for patients and must be managed at deployment.
For a health system evaluating an ECG foundation model, the disparity to plan for is age, and it is invisible in the headline number.
At a fixed threshold the type of error changes with age: a pooled threshold under-detects disease in the young and generates false alarms in the old, and calibration worsens with age.
Both are manageable with age-specific thresholds and per-band recalibration (Fig. 4E, F).
text.formatted: Both are manageable with age-specific thresholds and per-band recalibration (Fig. <ref type="figure">4E</ref>, <ref type="figure">F</ref>).

text.text: Three recommendations follow.
Model cards [28] and prediction-model reporting [24] should present age-stratified discrimination, miss rate and calibration as primary results.
text.formatted: Model cards <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">[28]</ref> and prediction-model reporting <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">[24]</ref> should present age-stratified discrimination, miss rate and calibration as primary results.

text.text: Because the gap persists across every backbone, an untrained network and a classical model, switching vendors will not resolve it, and any fairness evaluation of a foundation model should include an untrained copy and a classical baseline before attributing a gap to the model.
Deployments should use age-specific thresholds and recalibration, or at minimum report and monitor by age band.
Because the gap is present before any ECG pretraining and unchanged by larger labelled sets, demographically balanced pretraining and more labels are unlikely to close it on their own.

Remedies that act on the task are more promising, such as labels that depend less on non-ECG information (adjudicated rather than coded outcomes), decision thresholds defined within age strata, and explicit modelling of the age-dependent control distribution.
Any model-side gain should be measured against the untrained and classical baselines reported here, on held-out data, with an explicit accuracy-fairness trade-off.
Limitations.

The non-ECG references are two models from different architecture families, run (with the additional seeds) on subsets of at most 100,000 ECGs per cohort, and the untrained MOMENT copy reproduced the gaps less closely than the untrained ECG networks; the concordance that carries the argument is between models that share nothing.

Adaptation was evaluated as rank-8 LoRA on capped training sets rather than full fine-tuning, which is how frozen foundation models are adapted in practice, and the untrained and classical controls bound what any adaptation could reallocate.
Race labels exist only for the three US cohorts and are EHR-recorded categories, so the race results describe those health systems, where the gaps were small and unstable in direction.

LEAD has too few events under 40 years for the primary age-gap definition and enters the age analysis through the secondary 40-59 versus ≥75 gradient, on which it showed no decline with wide CIs and an oldest band limited to 75-80 years by its recruitment, while contributing fully to the overall external comparison.
Bootstrap CIs resample ECGs while folds are patient-grouped and are therefore somewhat narrow in cohorts with repeated ECGs, but no conclusion rests on a single interval.

The continental comparison is confounded with device and protocol [29], which is why every gap is estimated within a cohort; potassium is US-only; and ED-BWH's print-format waveforms required a 3-lead primary analysis, with which the 12-lead sensitivity analysis agrees.
text.formatted: The continental comparison is confounded with device and protocol <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">[29]</ref>, which is why every gap is estimated within a cohort; potassium is US-only; and ED-BWH's print-format waveforms required a 3-lead primary analysis, with which the 12-lead sensitivity analysis agrees.

text.text: Finally, the controls show that the gap is of similar size in untrained, classical and pretrained models, not that its avoidable component is zero.
